index.title: Solar Advisor — is PV worth it for your home?
index.h1: Is solar worth it for your home?
index.subtitle: A quick screening estimate for anywhere in Europe. Three short steps, no sign-up.
step1.city.hint: Used to pick the closest point in our European sunlight map.
step1.orientation: Which way does the roof face?
step1.roofArea.hint: Roughly the sunny part of the roof, ignoring chimneys and shading.
step1.consumption.hint: It is on your annual bill. A typical European home uses 3 000–5 000 kWh.
sizing.fromArea: That is roughly a {kwp} kWp system.
sizing.fromKwp: That needs roughly {area} m² of roof.
step2.lead: Defaults are typical values. Change any you know — your own bill is always better than our guess.
step2.retailPrice: What you pay for electricity (per kWh)
step2.feedInTariff: What you are paid for exports (per kWh)
step2.feedInTariff.hint: The gap between these two drives the whole battery question.
step2.batteryKwh.hint: Set to 0 to skip the battery. We always show you both cases.
step3.lead: Planning a heat pump, an electric car or air conditioning? Each one changes how much of your own solar you can use. Turn on any that apply — or none, and go straight to your results.
asset.hp.name: Heat pump
asset.hp.title: Heat pump — heating your home with electricity
asset.hp.hint: Uses the most electricity in winter, when there is least sun. Usually the toughest case for solar.
asset.ev.name: Electric car
asset.ev.title: Electric car — charging at home
asset.ev.hint: Adds a lot of demand. Whether it helps your solar depends entirely on when you charge.
evStrategy.dumb: Plug in when I get home (evening)
evStrategy.solar: Charge during the day, from my own solar
ev.strategy.hint: Daytime charging only helps if the car is actually parked at home on weekdays. For most commuters it is not.
asset.ac.name: Air conditioning
asset.ac.title: Air conditioning — cooling in summer
asset.ac.hint: Runs on hot, sunny afternoons — the one addition that usually fits solar well.

cta.h3: Not sure this is the right system?
cta.hint: Put two versions of it next to each other — with and without a battery, more or fewer panels, a heat pump or not. Your house and your tariffs carry over.
assump.screening: Screening estimate, not a quote. Treat these numbers as a first indication, not an engineering study or a financial promise. A proper design tool optimises the system; this one tests the system you described.
assump.uncosted: Only the panels and the battery are costed. Buying and installing a heat pump, an electric car or an air conditioner is not in any figure here — their effect on your electricity bill is, but their price is not. Nor are grants, subsidies, tax relief or the running costs of whatever the heat pump replaces.
assump.data: Sunlight and temperature are PVGIS measurements for {city} ({country}) itself. If you live well above or below the town — common in valleys and hill country — your own conditions will differ.
assump.hp: Heat pump: space heating only — hot water is not included, so a heat pump that also heats your water will use more. Its efficiency is calculated hour by hour and falls in cold weather, which is why the winter figures look worse than a single headline efficiency would suggest.
assump.ev: Electric car: the same amount is charged every day of the year, so holidays and long trips are averaged away. Daytime charging assumes the car is at home and plugged in on weekday afternoons.
assump.ac: Air conditioning: cooling is estimated from how far summer temperatures rise above {base} °C, not from your building's insulation or how you actually use it.
assump.load: Your electricity use is spread over the year using a typical household pattern scaled to the {consumption} you entered — not your real meter data. A household that is out all day will see less benefit than this; one at home during the day will see more.
assump.load.withExtras: Your electricity use is spread over the year using a typical household pattern scaled to the {consumption} you entered — not your real meter data. A household that is out all day will see less benefit than this; one at home during the day will see more. With your extras added, total use comes to {total} a year.
assump.fixed: The extras are tested against a fixed system. Switching a heat pump, car or air conditioner on never resizes the {kwp} kWp of panels — that is deliberate, so the change you see is the extra's doing and not a different system's. A larger system would usually suit a bigger household better.
assump.fixed.withBattery: The extras are tested against a fixed system. Switching a heat pump, car or air conditioner on never resizes the {kwp} kWp of panels or the {kwh} kWh battery — that is deliberate, so the change you see is the extra's doing and not a different system's. A larger system would usually suit a bigger household better.
assump.shading: No shading from trees, chimneys or neighbouring buildings is modelled.
assump.dispatch: Battery control is a simple rule: store surplus, use it when short. It does not trade on prices or plan ahead, so a smart system could do slightly better.
assump.weather: Weather variability between days is smoothed out, which makes the battery look slightly better than it would be in a real year. The typical-day charts are month averages for the same reason: a real day is spikier than either curve, so never read a peak or a fuse size off them.
assump.batteryIncremental: The battery is judged on what it adds, not on your whole bill: its cost is set against the extra solar it lets you keep instead of exporting. That makes the gap between your {retail}/kWh purchase price and your {feedIn}/kWh export price the number that decides it.
assump.money: Money: {years}-year life, {rate}% discount rate, panels losing 0.5% output per year, maintenance at 1% of system cost per year, electricity prices rising {escalation}% per year. All amounts are in the currency you selected; no exchange rates are applied. The money chart shows the plain running total, so it crosses zero at the payback year quoted above; the {npv} headline is the same cash flow discounted back to today, which is why the two figures differ.
assump.methodLink: This panel lists the caveats that apply to your scenario. The whole method — data sources, formulas and every limitation — is written out in how this works.

compare.title: Compare two systems — Solar Advisor
compare.subtitle: One house, two kits. Set the house up once, then put any two combinations of panels, battery and electric extras side by side.
compare.noState.lead: This page compares two systems for one particular house, so it needs to know the house first — where it is, which way the roof faces, and how much electricity it uses.
compare.house.lead: Carried over from your answers, and fixed for both columns — only the kit below changes.
compare.chart.title: Where the electricity came from
compare.chart.hint: Each bar is that month's total use.
compare.result.note: over {years} years, after paying for the kit
compare.energy.selfConsumption: Of your solar, used on site
compare.summary.panels: {kwp} kWp of panels — about {area} m² of roof
compare.notice.uncosted: What you pay for the {items} is not included. Only the panels and the battery are costed here. The extras change the electricity bill, and that is in every figure on this page — but the price of buying and installing them is not, so the value figures are not a full purchase decision for them.
compare.delta.identical: Both columns are the same system — change the panels, the battery or the extras on one side to see what it does.
compare.delta.better: {system} is worth {gap} more over the system's life.
compare.delta.betterClose: {system} is worth {gap} more over the system's life. That is close enough that the choice can rest on what you want rather than on the money.
compare.delta.row.selfConsumption: Of your solar, used on site
compare.delta.footnote: Both columns use the same house, the same weather and the same tariffs, so every difference above comes from the kit alone.
compare.assump.screening: Screening estimate, not a quote. Treat these as a first indication, not an engineering study or a financial promise.
compare.assump.uncosted: Only the panels and the battery are costed. Buying and installing a heat pump, an electric car or an air conditioner is not in any figure here — their effect on your electricity bill is, but their price is not.
compare.assump.data: Sunlight and temperature are PVGIS measurements for {city} ({country}) itself, and are identical for both columns.
compare.assump.kitOnly: Only the kit differs. Both columns share the house, the roof, the base electricity use and every tariff — that is what makes the comparison meaningful. To compare two towns or two tariffs, run the step-by-step version twice.
compare.assump.extras: The extras are added on top of the same base consumption, so a column with a heat pump legitimately uses more electricity than one without. Compare the yearly bill and the value over the system's life, not the self-sufficiency alone — adding a heat pump lowers self-sufficiency even when it saves money overall.
compare.assump.dispatch: Battery control is a simple rule: store surplus, use it when short. No price trading, no forecasting.
compare.assump.weather: Weather variability between days is smoothed out, which flatters the battery slightly in both columns.
compare.assump.money: Money: {years}-year life, {rate}% discount rate, panels losing 0.5% output per year, maintenance at 1% of system cost per year. All amounts are in the currency you selected; no exchange rates are applied.
